Les effets précis, les limitations et les conditions d'utilisation de ces Listes restent ceux prévus par MERP-RMU.

Les Chants de Contrôle et les Chants d'Inspiration possèdent une particularité importante : certains de leurs sorts exigent une véritable Manœuvre de Performance après le lancement magique. La qualité de cette performance influence les paramètres prévus par le sort. Le Meneur doit donc tenir compte des compétences artistiques réellement développées par le personnage, en conservant les mécanismes RMU.

La profession conserve une forte orientation vers les connaissances. Les Listes de base du Barde RMU comprennent les Chants d'Inspiration, qui remplacent l'ancienne Liste de Savoirs (Lores) utilisée dans des versions antérieures. Cette évolution ne diminue pas l'importance narrative du Barde comme gardien des traditions, puisque ses caractéristiques et ses compétences favorisent toujours la mémoire, l'étude des langues et les connaissances historiques.

Il convient de distinguer les traditions littéraires de Tolkien de leur représentation dans le système de jeu. Les figures de Daeron, Maglor, Lúthien ou Gléowine illustrent différents aspects de la musique en Terre du Milieu, mais ne correspondent pas nécessairement aux capacités d'un Barde défini par les règles RMU. Les chants de puissance accomplis par certains êtres exceptionnels ne doivent pas être considérés comme des facultés ordinaires de la profession.

Enfin, le Barde peut appartenir à des cultures très différentes. Son répertoire, les instruments qu'il emploie, ses connaissances historiques et sa manière d'exercer la magie doivent refléter les traditions de son peuple. Cette diversité permet d'incarner aussi bien un ménestrel du Gondor qu'un chanteur du Rohan, un gardien de mémoire dúnadan, un artiste elfe ou un conteur des régions orientales.

Le Barde prend toute sa dimension lorsque ses connaissances et sa magie contribuent à la vie de la compagnie, aux relations avec les autres peuples et à la conservation des événements qui marqueront les aventures des personnages.

Bard

Songs and the Memory of Peoples

Autumn is drawing to a close in the Westfold. For several days, cold rain has swept down from the White Mountains, and the roads linking the farms to the villages have become difficult to travel. At dusk, the last families make their way to a great timber hall surrounded by a few farm buildings. The horses have been led beneath the shelters, the doors have been shut, and thick smoke rises above the thatched roof.

Inside, several hearths illuminate the long tables where the inhabitants have taken their places. Bowls of soup pass from hand to hand, and the children have gathered around a man seated on a bench at the far end of the hall. A small harp rests upon his knees. His hair is beginning to turn grey, his cloak bears the marks of a long journey, and a short sword hangs from his belt.

For some fifteen years, the musician has attended the gatherings, weddings, and festivals of the villages of the Westfold. He knows the families, their old disputes, and the names of the men who have fallen in battle. He is welcomed whenever he returns after months away, for he brings news from Edoras, songs learned in other valleys, and tales entrusted to him by travellers met along the roads.

Tonight, however, the gathering is troubled. Riders have reported suspicious movements near the western lands, and two isolated farms have failed to send their wagons to the customary market. The master of the house wishes to know whether the families should abandon their lands before winter, while several young men demand an expedition against the raiders lurking nearby.

The Bard listens to the discussion without intervening. Then, as the meal draws to an end, he slowly tunes his harp and begins an ancient song of the days when Eorl's riders crossed the northern plains to come to Gondor's aid. Its verses recall the long ride, the hardships endured, and the men who left their homes behind to answer an ally's call.

Conversation ceases. The elders know the refrain, and several voices soon join the musician's. As the song unfolds, eyes turn towards the men sitting beside the master of the house. All have heard these verses since childhood, yet the tale reminds them of what the defence of a people may demand: courage, discipline, and the resolve to act together.

When the final notes fade, the Bard sets down his harp and asks leave to speak. He recounts the news gathered during his travels. A merchant from the western valleys spoke to him of unknown horsemen; a shepherd discovered traces of an abandoned encampment; farther north, a patrol was seen near an ancient crossing. The reports remain uncertain, but considered together they provide good reason to send scouts before any decision is made.

The man also knows a forgotten path leading into a neighbouring valley. He first learned of it from an old song preserved by a family of the region, and recognised its course during an earlier journey. Should the farms have to be evacuated, this passage would allow the families to reach safety without taking the main road.

The following morning, two riders will set out to reconnoitre the threatened lands. The inhabitants will begin gathering their provisions, and the younger folk will prepare shelters for the animals. As for the musician, he will accompany the scouts as far as the passage he has described.

In a few weeks, perhaps, he will take the road again towards Edoras or the northern valleys. He will carry with him the news of this village, the names of those who took part in its defence, and the events that future generations must remember.

For he is a Bard, and his art belongs as much to the memory of peoples as to the men and women to whom he lends his voice today.

The Memory of Peoples

In Middle-earth, songs and tales have accompanied the history of its peoples since the earliest times. They pass down the names of ancestors, preserve the memory of battles, and allow successive generations to learn of the events that shaped their lives. Stories told beside the hearth, laments sung over tombs, and poems recited in great halls belong to a tradition whose worth extends far beyond entertainment.

The Bard has a natural place in this inheritance. His training combines music, the spoken word, knowledge of languages, and the study of ancient tales. He learns to commit lengthy works to memory, to perform them before different audiences, and to recognise the occasions on which a particular story should be told. Some works celebrate the memory of a king or hero; others recall old alliances, migrations, and disasters whose remembrance has been preserved by the communities that endured them.

Such a responsibility demands a precise knowledge of tradition. A genealogy recited before a noble family touches upon the reputation of its ancestors. A song devoted to a battle must name those who distinguished themselves there, while also honouring the dead. In villages where written records are scarce, the Bard may preserve information that no one else could recount accurately.

Great houses and royal courts gladly receive artists able to celebrate their traditions. Yet the Bard also practises his art in the humblest places. A village assembly, an inn frequented by travellers, or a caravan's encampment offers him the opportunity to hear new tales and pass on those he knows.

His journeys thus give him a particular understanding of different peoples. He discovers the customs of their communities, learns local variations of songs, and gathers reports of recent events. Some become sought-after chroniclers; others spend their lives upon the roads, exchanging their art for hospitality and for whatever news their hosts are willing to share.

Their reputation rests as much upon the trust they inspire as upon their talent. A skilfully fashioned tale may reconcile two families, whereas an ill-judged word can revive an old quarrel. Experience gradually teaches the Bard to weigh the consequences of the stories he passes on and to choose the occasions when they should be heard.

The Ancient Songs of Middle-earth

Music holds a fundamental place in Tolkien's world. At the very beginning of Arda, the Great Music of the Ainur precedes the shaping of the world. This conception lends song a particular depth, echoes of which endure within the traditions of the Elves.

In the First Age, Daeron, minstrel and loremaster at Thingol's court, ranks among the greatest musicians of the Eldar. In the halls of Menegroth, his music accompanies Lúthien's dancing, and he takes part in the cultural life of the realm of Doriath. He is also credited with devising the first runes known as the Cirth, testimony to the breadth of his knowledge.

Among the Noldor, Maglor, son of Fëanor, enjoys comparable renown. His songs preserve the memory of the suffering and events that shaped his people. After the tragedies in which he played a part, his long wandering takes him along the shores of Middle-earth, singing of sorrow and regret. His story shows how closely music can remain bound to the life of the one who composes it.

Other works arise from the desire to preserve the memory of those who are gone. The Narn i Chîn Húrin, attributed to the poet Dírhaval, recounts the tragic fate of the children of Húrin. Thus the great compositions of the Elder Days become historical testimonies, preserved and taken up by the generations that follow.

Tolkien's tales also speak of songs whose power surpasses that of ordinary works. The contest between Finrod Felagund and Sauron at Tol-in-Gaurhoth takes the form of a struggle in which words and music bear tremendous forces. Lúthien's songs likewise possess extraordinary power, notably when she succeeds in putting Morgoth to sleep within his own stronghold.

Such manifestations, however, belong to exceptional beings and circumstances. They reveal the power that music may attain in Middle-earth without making every poet or singer a practitioner of such enchantments.

In the Third Age, the tradition endures among Men, Dwarves, and Hobbits. In their songs, the Rohirrim preserve the memory of kings and great rides. Gléowine, Théoden's minstrel, composes a lament after the War of the Ring that will be sung at the king's funeral in Edoras. In the same age, the songs of the Dwarves recall the greatness of Khazad-dûm, while Bilbo and the Hobbits sustain a tradition of popular songs, poems, and family tales.

The Bard draws his identity from this diversity. His profession is one whose knowledge and powers take on different meanings according to the traditions that have shaped him.

Learning the Arts of Speech and Music

The Bard's education often begins in childhood, when a master notices a young pupil's aptitude for singing, memorisation, or storytelling. In some cultures, the apprenticeship takes place within a family of musicians; elsewhere, a travelling performer agrees to train a disciple who will accompany him for several years.

The first lessons concern command of the voice and rhythm. The pupil learns to sustain a melody, control his breathing, and articulate words clearly. If he plays an instrument, daily exercises gradually develop the precision of his movements. Such training requires long hours of repetition, far removed from the apparent ease with which accomplished artists perform before an audience.

Memorisation forms an essential part of his education. His master entrusts him with increasingly lengthy songs, historical accounts, and genealogies, all of which he must reproduce without altering their important details. Some texts exist in several versions, each preserving the customs or memories of a particular community. The young Bard thus discovers that differences between two accounts may reveal ancient events, rivalries, or traditions whose origins reach back through many generations.

The study of languages is likewise part of his apprenticeship. A minstrel who intends to travel must understand the expressions used in the regions he crosses and know how to adapt his art to varied audiences. Some acquire a remarkable familiarity with ancient tongues, particularly when they seek to interpret Elvish works or songs preserved by the descendants of Númenor.

Composition gradually completes these studies. The pupil learns to structure a tale, select images and rhythms suited to his purpose, and alter his performance to suit the occasion. A lament demands a solemnity different from a song intended for a feast. Before warriors, an ancient lay may emphasise the circumstances of a battle; among a bereaved family, those same events will be recalled through the memory of those who died.

The master also attaches great importance to conduct in the company of others. A Bard's reputation depends upon his ability to listen, respect local customs, and recognise the people he addresses. A skilful performer knows how to observe an audience, understand its reactions, and adapt his delivery without compromising the meaning of the work.

Magical instruction is gradually incorporated into this education. Mastery of Essence demands an additional discipline, enabling the Bard to associate certain supernatural effects with the voice, sound, or performance. The young practitioner learns to distinguish the ordinary qualities of his art from the powers that magic allows him to wield.

By the end of his apprenticeship, he possesses knowledge whose value extends well beyond artistic talent. He understands customs, languages, ancient events, and the means of holding an audience's attention. His travels and encounters will continue to enrich that knowledge throughout his life.

The Traditions of the Peoples

The Bard's place varies considerably among the cultures of Middle-earth.

Among the Elves, music remains intimately bound to memory and to the beauty of the world. A Sindarin singer may preserve tales reaching back to the vanished realms of Beleriand, while a Noldorin musician may devote himself to the great compositions of his people and to events whose last witnesses are still alive. The longevity of the Eldar allows works to be passed down over many centuries, sometimes in the company of those who composed them. The traditions of Lórien and Rivendell also provide a particularly favourable setting for such instruction.

Among the Dúnedain, the Bard helps preserve a heritage marked by the loss of Númenor and the wars of the kingdoms that succeeded it. In Gondor, he may be attached to a noble house, take part in public ceremonies, or devote his studies to ancient chronicles. In the North, where the memory of Arnor survives among scattered communities, the transmission of tales holds particular importance. A song learned from an elder may be the last surviving testimony to a family's tradition.

In Rohan, sung verse accompanies life in the great halls, assemblies, and funeral rites. Poems celebrate the kings, the riders, and the events that shaped the history of the Mark. A Bard of this culture knows the genealogies, old alliances, and accounts of battles. His art remains closely associated with the values of courage, loyalty, and hospitality handed down by his people.

The Dwarves likewise possess rich musical traditions. Their songs tell of lineages, the labours of craftsmen, lost treasures, and the ancient dwellings of their people. The Song of Durin, which Gimli sings in Moria, recalls the splendour of the underground kingdom and the grief of its loss. A Khazâd Bard may thus become the keeper of tales passed down within his House, attaching particular importance to the accuracy of names and events.

Among the Hobbits, music is thoroughly woven into everyday life. Festivals, meals, and family gatherings give rise to songs, some of which have been handed down for generations. Tales of journeys, humorous compositions, and genealogies hold a considerable place in their traditions. A Hobbit Bard may develop a remarkable gift for composition and storytelling while practising his profession in surroundings more familiar than those of the great courts.

The Dorwinrim, the merchants of Rhovanion, and the peoples of the southern regions offer other possibilities. In trading settlements, performers gather news brought by caravans and meet travellers from distant lands. In Umbar, music accompanies the celebrations of great houses and may serve the ambitions of those who maintain them. The peoples of the East and South have traditions of their own, whose instruments, rhythms, and poetic forms may differ profoundly from those of the West.

These origins give the Bard particular responsibilities and habits. Some regard their art as a sacred inheritance; others see it as a trade, a way of serving their community, or a means of pursuing an independent life. Their education naturally influences the works they choose and the place they accord to magic.

Roads, Halls, and Gatherings

The Bard's life often depends upon his reputation and the places where he practises his art. Some hold a permanent position at a court or in the household of an important family, while others spend much of the year upon the roads. They attend fairs, celebrations, and gatherings whose dates they know, returning at every stage to hosts who have welcomed them for many years.

Travel forms an essential part of their continuing education. A musician passing through an unfamiliar region discovers songs he has never heard, recent events, and tales the inhabitants have preserved for generations. Caravans, inns, and harbours become favoured places in which to gather such knowledge.

This way of life calls for practical skills. The Bard must maintain his instruments, protect his manuscripts from damp, and ensure that he has the resources needed to reach his next destination. When travelling alone, he learns to recognise dangerous roads and defend himself against ordinary threats. Some become familiar with the use of a sword or bow, particularly when accompanying soldiers or merchants.

The welcome he receives depends upon his reputation and local custom. In some communities, a singer's arrival is eagerly awaited; elsewhere, strangers arouse a distrust that even his talent may dispel only after several meetings. He must therefore observe accepted practices, choose suitable tales, and avoid words that might needlessly wound his hosts.

Festivals and great ceremonies require particular skill. A wedding may bring together families whose relations remain delicate. An assembly of warriors expects songs that celebrate the deeds of its leaders. At funerals, the bereaved entrust the Bard with recalling a life whose memory they wish to preserve.

Such responsibilities bind his art closely to the lives of the communities he visits. His songs accompany joyful occasions, but also those moments when people seek to understand the losses they have just suffered. The trust placed in an experienced Bard often grows from his repeated presence at such times.

The Magic of Voice and Sound

The Bard's magic belongs to the realm of Essence. It extends his artistic abilities by allowing him to employ the voice, music, and the properties of sound for extraordinary purposes.

Song is the most characteristic medium of this tradition, but bardic performances need not be confined to vocal music. A spoken recitation, an instrumental composition, or another mastered form of expression may accompany certain teachings, according to the possibilities allowed by the spells.

The effectiveness of this magic rests both upon knowledge of the powers involved and upon the quality of their performance. Certain spell lists require an actual performance after the spell has been cast. The character's artistic skill then directly influences the effects obtained, in accordance with the rules governing these enchantments.

This feature makes training especially important. A singer whose voice carries easily through a great hall does not necessarily possess the concentration required to sustain a magical effect. Conversely, a practitioner who knows his spells perfectly must still learn to accompany them with a performance suited to their demands.

The voice thus becomes an instrument of power as well as a means of expression. A Bard may bolster his companions' courage, encourage particular reactions in an audience, or employ the properties of sound to produce unusual effects. Other powers allow him to obtain information about objects and enrich the investigations in which he takes part.

Such magic has a natural place in Middle-earth, where certain songs possess extraordinary force. Lúthien's deeds and Finrod's contest against Sauron bear witness to the heights this art may reach. The abilities available to a Bard, however, remain those granted by his profession and level of experience; the exceptional manifestations of the great tales belong to a different order of power.

The manner in which he practises this magic ultimately depends upon his personality. Some seek striking effects capable of impressing an assembly. Others favour subtle enchantments, joined to performances whose listeners chiefly remember their beauty or emotional power.

The Six Paths of the Bard

The Bard's magical teachings are organised into six Base Spell Lists. They combine influence exerted through performance, the manipulation of sound, and the pursuit of knowledge.

Controlling Songs allow the Bard to influence certain reactions within an audience through performance. This discipline demands particular mastery of delivery, for the magical effect depends upon the conditions specified by the spell and, where required, the quality of the artistic performance. A Bard who develops this path becomes especially attentive to the ways in which words, rhythms, and emotions affect those who listen.

Entertaining Ways support different forms of performance. They allow the practitioner to improve certain aspects of his art and make use of his artistic abilities in a range of circumstances. This List is particularly well suited to minstrels, storytellers, and performers who regularly appear before an audience.

Inspiring Songs are devoted to the beneficial effects a performance can have upon those who witness it. They may, in particular, sustain or encourage an audience according to the powers employed. Within a company of adventurers, this discipline gives the Bard a distinctive place, associating his presence with his companions' confidence and resolve.

Item Lore opens a different field of study. It allows the practitioner to obtain certain information about the nature and properties of the objects he examines. This ability is of particular interest to Bards devoted to ancient tales, family inheritances, and the search for treasures or historical evidence.

Sound Control concerns the manipulation of particular properties of sound. Its powers allow the Bard to act upon sounds more directly than songs of influence, altering their characteristics according to the effects available. This discipline offers varied applications, from artistic performances to situations in which control of noise is especially important.

Finally, Sound Projection allows the Bard to extend, displace, or strengthen certain sounds. A Bard who develops these teachings gains remarkable means of making his voice heard, conveying sounds, or producing effects beyond the ordinary capabilities of his instrument.

These Lists may receive different priorities according to the character's training and responsibilities. A court minstrel may favour Controlling Songs and Entertaining Ways, while a performer accompanying soldiers may pursue Inspiring Songs more deeply. A scholar dedicated to preserving ancient traditions may attach particular importance to Item Lore.

The diversity of these teachings allows Bards of very different talents to be created, while preserving a common identity grounded in art, memory, and mastery of Essence.

Objects, Tales, and Secrets

Knowledge of objects has a particular place in the Bard's life. Weapons passed down within a family, jewels preserved for generations, and ancient musical instruments often carry histories of which their owners no longer know every detail.

A Bard summoned to a noble household may recognise the devices engraved upon a sword or discover, in a chronicle, the name of the person who once bore it. His historical knowledge enables him to place the object within its proper age, while certain magical powers give him access to information that would otherwise be difficult to obtain.

This union of scholarship and magic proves especially valuable in regions marked by ancient wars. The ruins of Arnor, the abandoned settlements of Gondor, and the remains of vanished cities preserve objects whose significance has been lost. An instrument found in a collapsed chamber, an almost illegible inscription, or fragments of a song may provide the first clues in a historical investigation.

Oral traditions complement such research. An apparently unremarkable tale may preserve the memory of a lost road, an ancient refuge, or an event whose circumstances have been forgotten. Knowledge of the variants of a single story then becomes valuable. A changed name, a missing stanza, or an unusual geographical reference may reveal where a song originated and help explain what it conveys.

The Bard must nevertheless learn to distinguish historical fact from embellishments added over time. Some songs were composed to celebrate a patron, others to justify a family's claims or preserve a particular tradition. Their value remains considerable, but interpreting them requires close attention to the circumstances in which they arose.

This search may become the work of an entire lifetime. A Bard sometimes discovers that a piece handed down for generations exists in several contradictory versions. Tracing their origins, meeting the last keepers of a tradition, and understanding the events that caused the differences provide ample reason to travel to distant lands.

Words in the Service of Others

The Bard's talent gives him a distinctive place in human affairs. Accustomed to observing the reactions of an audience, he recognises when an assembly is growing anxious, when a discussion threatens to turn into a quarrel, or when a speech begins to win over its listeners.

This experience allows him to intervene in many circumstances. A lord requests his presence at an important reception, a merchant values his ability to entertain guests, while a community leader asks him to recall the ancient commitments binding several families together. His memory of customs and oaths may lend his words particular authority.

The Bard also understands the value of personal stories. A tale shared among travelling companions may bring together people who previously knew nothing of one another. Songs handed down within a family preserve the memory of the departed, and words spoken during a ceremony help those present find a common meaning in the events they have experienced.

Yet this power of influence can become a source of conflict. An artist attached to a noble house may be asked to celebrate deeds of which he disapproves or ridicule his patron's enemies. A song composed to recall an ancient event may be taken as a political accusation, particularly when the families concerned do not share the same account of what happened.

The Bard must therefore weigh his commitments. Some choose to place their art at the service of a lord to whom they remain loyal, while others prefer to preserve their independence. Travelling performers enjoy greater freedom, but depend upon their listeners' hospitality and their ability to earn trust.

Magic brings an additional responsibility. Controlling Songs can influence certain reactions by supernatural means. The character must then decide under what circumstances he is willing to employ such power, especially when it affects people who do not realise they are subject to an enchantment.

This question lends the profession particular depth. The artist already knows the ordinary means of moving an audience; magic gives him the possibility of acting with even greater force. The manner in which he uses this gift often reveals his convictions and the limits he chooses to respect.

Songs in the Face of the Shadow

In a Middle-earth marked by war and the advance of the Shadow, songs sometimes become instruments of resistance. Threatened communities preserve the memory of their ancestors and the trials they endured. Poems of ancient victories recall that mighty enemies have been faced before, while laments preserve the memory of those who fell.

The Bard helps keep these traditions alive. His presence among travellers, soldiers, and displaced families allows him to pass on tales that give people a sense of belonging to a greater history. Some songs sustain the courage of fighters, while others bring precious comfort to survivors of disaster.

Memory, however, may also become a source of suffering when it remains bound to ancient hatreds. A song composed after a war sometimes preserves the accusations, humiliations, and desire for vengeance of those who passed it down. A Bard performing such a work must know the circumstances of its creation and understand the reactions it may provoke.

Servants of the Shadow may likewise seek to employ speech and music to extend their influence. False tales, seductive promises, and compositions intended to glorify a powerful master offer ways of turning loyalties aside or inflaming passions. An ambitious artist may be tempted to accept the patronage of a lord whose intentions remain obscure, especially when that lord promises him renown and the means to pursue his work.

The magic of Essence carries other dangers. Certain powers allow the Bard to influence an audience directly or manipulate sounds in circumstances where secrecy is especially valuable. Employing them for deception or domination may gradually draw him away from the responsibilities he once accepted.

The ancient tales also remind us that the power of song depends upon the will of the one who employs it. Finrod confronts Sauron through music and words, yet his adversary also possesses the power to shape a song of terrible strength. Beauty of expression is therefore no guarantee of righteous intention.

For a Bard, this confrontation between memory, influence, and truth may become one of the defining struggles of his life. He must choose which events he wishes to pass down, the causes to which he lends his voice, and the powers he is willing to employ.

The Bard Through the Ages

The Bard's place depends profoundly upon the age in which the campaign is set.

In the First Age, the great musical traditions of the Elves provide a particularly rich setting. A Sindarin Bard may live at the court of Thingol, where Daeron serves as minstrel and loremaster. Among the Noldor, the art of song likewise belongs to a culture shaped by tales of the earliest days and the tragedies of exile. The wars against Morgoth give rise to many laments, while the human communities of Beleriand preserve the memory of battles and migrations. The character may become a witness to events whose songs will endure for centuries.

In the Second Age, the rise of Númenor makes it possible to imagine Bards trained among noble families, scholars, and musicians attached to the island's great houses. Sea voyages and relations with the peoples of Middle-earth encourage encounters between different traditions. As Númenor turns away from the Eldar, some artists remain faithful to their ancient inheritance, while others place their talents at the service of the kings' growing ambitions. After the Downfall, the survivors pass their tales on to the communities established in Arnor and Gondor.

In the Third Age, the profession has a place in widely differing cultures. The minstrels of Rohan preserve the lays of kings and riders; in Gondor, court performers take part in ceremonies and pass on the histories of great families. The Dúnedain of the North preserve the memory of vanished kingdoms, while the Elves maintain the songs of the Elder Days. Among Dwarves and Hobbits, songs accompany everyday life and recall the founding events of their communities. The advance of the Shadow makes the transmission of tales of courage, alliance, and loyalty especially precious.

In the Fourth Age, the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom opens new possibilities. Ancient roads become accessible once more, exchanges between peoples increase, and archives preserved through the years of war can be brought together. A Bard helps pass down the memory of the War of the Ring, celebrate the restoration of the kingdoms, and preserve the tales of peoples whose presence in Middle-earth is beginning to diminish. New generations thus inherit a body of memories that they must learn to interpret and carry forward.

Each age lends a particular meaning to the character's vocation. A Bard of the First Age may witness the great tragedies of Beleriand; one of the Second Age accompanies the rise and fall of Númenor. In the Third Age, he often preserves a threatened inheritance, while his successor in the Fourth helps recount the events that have just transformed Middle-earth for generations to come.

Leaving the Hall

The Bard's life naturally leads him to travel. Even when he has a home and patrons, his education encourages him to meet other performers, seek out ancient works, and gather accounts of events whose memory he wishes to preserve.

Some set out in search of a renowned master or to learn a musical tradition unknown in their homeland. Others seek a lost manuscript, the words of a song whose melody alone has survived, or the last descendants of a family whose history they wish to reconstruct.

Circumstances may also force a departure. War has destroyed the home where the character practised his art; a patron has died and his heirs no longer wish to maintain a minstrel; a composition has provoked a dispute that obliges him to leave the region. Some Bards depart after discovering that a tale handed down over generations conceals events very different from those they were taught.

Adventure also offers them the chance to take part directly in stories they would once have merely recounted. A Bard accompanies a company sent to recover an ancient object, enters the service of a leader whose convictions he admires, or joins travellers whose expedition promises to carry him into lands seldom described.

Life on the road demands skills unlike those developed in great halls. Long marches, foul weather, and combat test his endurance and equipment. Yet the experience he has gained among travellers helps him adapt. He knows the customs of hospitality, can begin a conversation, and recognises occasions when a familiar song will ease the mood of a gathering.

Within a company, the Bard contributes his knowledge of peoples, languages, and history. His magical powers support his companions, aid certain investigations, and allow him to employ sound in extraordinary ways. His artistic and social abilities prove useful both among those met along the road and in situations where the adventurers must negotiate or seek assistance.

The relationships formed during these journeys gradually change the way he tells the world's stories. Tales handed down by his masters acquire new meaning when he discovers the places where they unfolded. His companions entrust him with their memories, hopes, and sometimes events they had previously preferred to keep secret. The character must then decide what he will keep to himself and what deserves to be passed on.

When he returns, the Bard possesses new songs, but also personal experience that lends a different depth to his art. The events in which he took part may one day join the tales he hands down to future generations.

Playing a Bard

The Bard offers the opportunity to portray a character whose talents rest upon memory, artistic expression, and knowledge of other peoples. His cultural origins, however, determine how these qualities manifest themselves and what place he accords to magic.

A young minstrel of Rohan may have grown up under a master attached to the court of Edoras, learning the lays of kings and the ancient songs of the Mark. A musician of Gondor may preserve works handed down by her family for generations, while a Dúnadan of the North travels through Eriador gathering the tales of scattered communities. A Dwarven singer may search for the remains of an ancestral dwelling, while a Hobbit may prefer festivals, humorous poems, and stories told beside the hearth.

The character's relationships with his master, loved ones, and patrons offer many possibilities. Has he inherited an ancient instrument whose history he does not yet fully know? Is a song bound to the memory of someone who has died? Did a lord once ask him to compose a work he refused to write? Is there a tale whose original version he longs to recover, despite the interests of those who would rather see it forgotten?

His character will depend largely upon his experience. Some Bards readily seek the company of others and enjoy lively conversation. Others possess a reserve that contrasts with the confidence they display when performing before an audience. The habit of being listened to can foster excessive self-assurance, while dealings with powerful figures sometimes teach remarkable caution.

His relationship with magic likewise deserves particular attention. One Bard may regard his powers as a natural extension of his art, passed down alongside musical techniques. Another sees them as a demanding discipline, reserved for important occasions. Some seek to deepen their mastery of Inspiring Songs in order to support their companions, while others are fascinated by the possibilities offered by powers of influence.

The profession is particularly well suited to campaigns centred on travel, relations between communities, the search for ancient knowledge, and historical events whose consequences endure across generations. It also has a natural place in adventures where characters must negotiate, preserve an alliance, or understand the traditions of the peoples they encounter.

Over the course of his life, the Bard discovers that the most important tales are sometimes those in which he himself has taken part. His choices then determine the place he will hold in the stories he passes down, and the memory his companions will preserve of him.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Bard in MERP-RMU

The Bard is a semi-spell user of Essence, whose abilities combine Performance Arts, Lore, Languages, Communication, Influence, and certain martial skills.

His prime characteristics are Memory (Me) and Presence (Pr). Memory represents his ability to retain tales, languages, songs, and genealogies. Presence governs his relationship with an audience and the force of his performances. His realm of magic remains Essence, in accordance with the RMU framework employed by the module.

He has six Base Spell Lists:

ListDomain
Controlling SongsInfluence exerted upon an audience through performance
Entertaining WaysSupport and improvement of artistic performances
Inspiring SongsEncouragement and strengthening of those attending the performance
Item LoreGathering information about objects and their properties
Sound ControlManipulation of the characteristics of sound
Sound ProjectionExtension, displacement, and strengthening of sounds

The precise effects, limitations, and conditions of use of these Lists remain those provided by MERP-RMU.

Controlling Songs and Inspiring Songs share an important feature: certain spells require an actual Performance Maneuver after the spell has been cast. The quality of that performance influences the parameters specified by the spell. The Gamemaster must therefore take account of the artistic skills the character has actually developed, while retaining the RMU mechanics.

The profession maintains a strong emphasis on knowledge. The RMU Bard's Base Lists include Inspiring Songs, which replaces the earlier Lores List employed in previous versions. This change does not diminish the Bard's narrative importance as a guardian of tradition, since his characteristics and skills continue to favour memory, the study of languages, and historical knowledge.

It is important to distinguish Tolkien's literary traditions from their representation in the game system. Figures such as Daeron, Maglor, Lúthien, and Gléowine illustrate different aspects of music in Middle-earth, but do not necessarily correspond to the capabilities of a Bard as defined by RMU rules. Songs of power performed by certain exceptional beings should not be regarded as ordinary abilities of the profession.

Finally, a Bard may belong to widely differing cultures. His repertoire, the instruments he uses, his historical knowledge, and his manner of practising magic should reflect the traditions of his people. This diversity makes it possible to portray a minstrel of Gondor, a singer of Rohan, a Dúnadan keeper of memory, an Elven performer, or a storyteller from the eastern regions.

The Bard comes fully into his own when his knowledge and magic enrich the life of the company, its relations with other peoples, and the preservation of the events that will shape the adventurers' stories.
